items.answer: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.
Pose is the position and orientation of a viewer or tracked object.

The Microsoft HoloLens is an augmented reality headset and a see-through display that integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through special glasses. Interaction takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

Augmented virtuality is the intermediate state on the reality-virtuality continuum, opposite augmented reality, in which a virtual environment is augmented with real-world images, videos, or live capture appearing in real time.

questions.question: In an XR system, what kind of part is tracking?
options: An integral hardware component
A software tracking component
A display rendering component
An audio synchronization component
questions.explanation: Tracking is an integral hardware component of an XR system. It is not a software, display, or audio component.

questions.question: How does the main focus of tracking differ between virtual reality and augmented reality?
options: VR tracks the physical environment to replace the real world, while AR tracks virtual motion to update the view
VR registers virtual content in real space, while AR translates user motion into virtual motion
VR translates user motion into virtual motion, while AR registers virtual content in real space
VR tracks the user's virtual motion, while AR tracks the user's real motion
questions.explanation: VR tracking is primarily about turning the user's physical motion or input into motion in the virtual world. AR tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in 3D space relative to real-world anchors.

questions.question: In XR, how is tracking related to sensing?
options: Tracking names the software side, while sensing names the hardware side
Sensing is a display task, while tracking is a rendering task
They name different activities, and sensing is the more common term
They name the same activity, and tracking is the more common term
questions.explanation: Tracking is also commonly called sensing, but tracking is the more popular term for the activity. The devices that enable it are more often called sensors.

data.text: Tracking is an integral hardware component of XR systems, and keeping track of physical motion is crucial there, especially in VR. In VR, this tracking translates the user's physical motion or input into motion in the virtual world. In AR, the purpose shifts to registering virtual 3D content against a real-world anchor while also tracking the user's pose, position, orientation, and moving real-world objects in the field of view. The same capability is also called sensing, although the enabling devices are more often called sensors than trackers.
points: Tracking is an integral XR hardware component and is crucial for keeping track of physical motion, especially in VR.
In VR, tracking captures the user's physical motion or input and translates it into motion in the virtual world.
In AR, tracking registers virtual content in 3D space with respect to an anchor in the real world.
AR tracking also tracks the user's pose, position, and orientation, plus moving real-world objects in the field of view.
Tracking, the more popular term, is also called sensing; its devices are more often called sensors than trackers.

questions.question: Why does an XR system need to track the position and orientation of the user's sense organs?
options: so virtual audio can be raised when the ears turn toward a sound source
so the headset can replace external cameras used for outside-in tracking
so a display attached to them is perceived as attached to the surrounding world
so the user's walking speed can be used to adjust rendering resolution
questions.explanation: Sense organs such as eyes and ears have body-controlled degrees of freedom, so their position and orientation must be tracked to keep an attached display perceived as tied to the world. Tracking them is not primarily about replacing sensors, adjusting rendering from speed, or changing audio volume.

questions.question: In VR, for what reason may eye tracking be needed?
options: to register digital content with a moved object in an augmented reality view
to replace head tracking for the visual and aural components
to identify the position of external room sensors in an outside-in tracking setup
to compensate for eye movements required by the rendering or display technology
questions.explanation: Eye tracking may be needed when the rendering or display technology requires compensation for eye movements. Head tracking already serves the usual visual and aural components in VR, while locating room sensors or registering AR content are different tracking needs.

questions.question: Why is exact, perfect matching not required when a user's hands or face are tracked for a virtual representation?
options: because the virtual world already contains a permanent model of the user
because an approximate movement can still reproduce the body-part motion well enough
because external room sensors can replace body-part tracking in a virtual reality setup
because a button press can directly set a fixed grasp or pose
questions.explanation: Tracking other body parts does not require perfect matching; an approximate virtual reproduction of the movement can still give a good experience. A button press is a limiting case for setting a fixed configuration, not the general reason approximate tracking is acceptable.

questions.question: In VR, why must a physical wall around the user be tracked rather than relying on the user's pose?
options: because the user's head pose alone can show where the virtual room boundary ends
because the user's eye movements must be matched to the wall for sound
because the wall must be detected as a physical object missing from the virtual world
because the wall must serve as an anchor for digital content in an augmented reality view
questions.explanation: A wall not represented in the virtual world must itself be tracked so the user can be alerted to it and reduce harm. Tracking the user's pose alone does not reveal that physical object, and anchoring digital content is an AR concern.

data.text: Tracking in extended reality is divided by what is tracked: the user's sense organs, other body parts, and the surrounding environment. Sense-organ tracking keeps the virtual world aligned with the user's eyes and ears, while other-body-part tracking gives a usable virtual representation of the user. Environment tracking connects the virtual or digital experience to real objects, supporting augmented reality placement, virtual reality safety or touch, and telepresence.
points: Tracking in extended reality is categorized by what is tracked: sense organs, other body parts, and the environment.
Sense-organ tracking updates the virtual world because displays move with the user; virtual reality mostly tracks the head, sometimes eyes.
Other-body-part tracking adds avatars or gestures to the virtual world; approximate matching or simple input can suffice.
Environment tracking aligns augmented reality content, alerts or gives touch feedback in virtual reality, and supports telepresence live capture.

questions.question: Which factors decide the tracking method or technique that is applied?
options: The tracker position, the tracking process, and the tracker types
The tracker position, the tracking process, and the display types
The user position, the tracking process, and the tracker types
The tracker position, the display process, and the tracker types
questions.explanation: The choice of tracking technique depends on where the tracker is placed, the tracking process involved, and the kind of tracker used. Changing one of these factors to a display or user attribute does not match the stated basis for the choice.

questions.question: In outside-in tracking, where does the data for identifying the user's motion come from?
options: Cameras built into the head-mounted display send that data to the system attached to the user
External sensors in the real world send that data to the system attached to the user
Sensors worn on the user's body send that data to the system attached to the user
Anchors in the virtual environment send that data to the system attached to the user
questions.explanation: Outside-in tracking relies on trackers or sensors placed outside the experience device, such as cameras or markers in the real world, to help the user-attached system track motion and pose. Cameras in the HMD describe inside-out tracking, not outside-in tracking.

questions.question: What removes the fixed-area restriction found in outside-in tracking?
options: A pre-scanned virtual environment removes that restriction
External sensors with a wider range remove that restriction
External sensors placed in a larger room remove that restriction
Sensors attached to the user or the user's device remove that restriction
questions.explanation: Inside-out tracking avoids the fixed-area restriction because the tracking sensors are worn by the user or located in the user's experience device. More external range or a pre-scanned virtual environment does not change the fact that outside-in tracking still depends on a sensor-covered area.

data.text: Tracking choices depend on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types. Tracker position separates tracking into outside-in and inside-out approaches. Outside-in tracking relies on external trackers or sensors and is limited to their range, while inside-out tracking puts sensors in the user's experience device and needs no external tracking devices.
points: The tracking method depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.
Tracking is categorized as outside-in or inside-out according to tracker position.
Outside-in tracking uses external trackers or sensors, not the user's experience device, to determine motion, pose, and orientation.
Outside-in tracking works only within its sensor range, while inside-out tracking puts sensors in the user's experience device.

questions.question: What are the two broad ways to obtain input for tracking?
options: tracking with markers and tracking with displays
inside-out tracking and outside-in tracking
tracking of sense organs and tracking of body parts
tracking of the user and tracking of the environment
questions.explanation: Tracking input is broadly obtained either from sensors on the experience device or from external sensors in the real world. The other options describe what may be tracked, not how the tracking input is obtained.

questions.question: Why is calibration performed in a tracking process?
options: To merge many readings from different sources into one estimate
To find where the sensor is before any movement begins
To make imperfect sensor output approximate the real value
To switch from external trackers to trackers on the user
questions.explanation: Calibration corrects the output of imperfect sensors so it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value. It does not establish a starting pose, combine measurements, or change the sensor arrangement.

questions.question: What does drift correction reduce in tracking?
options: The difference between the separate sensor readings and the combined pose orientation
The difference between raw sensor readings and the natural head orientation
The difference between the unknown starting pose and the known initial orientation
The difference between estimated and actual position and orientation
questions.explanation: Drift correction compensates for the gap between estimated and actual position and orientation. The other options describe raw sensor error, initial pose setup, and sensor fusion, not drift correction.

data.text: Tracking obtains input by either inside-out or outside-in methods. The tracking process then consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration and registration prepare movement tracking by reducing sensor error and determining the sensor’s starting position and orientation, while integration combines measurements from multiple sources and drift correction reduces the difference between estimated and actual position and orientation.
points: Tracking input can be obtained in two broad ways: inside-out and outside-in.
The tracking process consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
Before movement tracking, calibration reduces sensor error, and registration determines the sensor’s starting position and orientation.
Integration aggregates measurements from multiple sources at discrete time points to track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.
Drift correction compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error.

activities.title: Order the stages of the tracking process

items.title: Order the stages of the tracking process
steps: Sensor output is transformed toward the natural value
The sensor's position and orientation are determined
Measurements from multiple sensors are aggregated at time points
The difference between estimated and actual pose is compensated

questions.question: How does the main purpose of tracking differ between virtual reality and augmented reality?
questions.reference_answer: In virtual reality, tracking is primarily about translating the user's physical motion or input into virtual motion in the virtual world. In augmented reality, tracking registers virtual content in three-dimensional space with respect to a real-world anchor. It therefore also requires the user's pose, position, and orientation and tracking of moving real-world objects in the field of view.

questions.question: How does the placement of sensors in outside-in tracking explain its range limitation compared with inside-out tracking?
questions.reference_answer: Outside-in tracking relies on external sensors or markers in the real world, not on sensors inside the user's experience device. Because those external sensors are placed in a specific area, the system works only when the user is within their sensor range. Inside-out tracking puts the needed cameras or other sensors within the experience device, such as a head-mounted display, so the user wears the sensors and does not have that placement restriction.

questions.question: Why is tracking the environment itself, rather than only the user, needed in virtual reality when a physical wall is not represented in the virtual world?
questions.reference_answer: Tracking the user is not useful for alerting the user to a physical object that is not represented in the virtual world. Tracking the environment itself can detect that physical object, such as a wall, and alert the user, reducing harm. In addition, the tracked physical object may be matched in the virtual world so the user receives touch feedback while interacting with it.
